cues.text: A Break-In on a Summer Night

On the night of July 25, 1969, thieves broke into the parish church of San Mauro La Bruca, a small village in the Cilento region of southern Italy, intent on stealing whatever valuables they could carry off.
Among their targets were the relics of the town's patron saints and a golden ciborium kept in the tabernacle, holding a number of consecrated Hosts.
Once outside the church, the thieves emptied the ciborium of its Hosts, discarding them onto a low wall by the side door and keeping only the precious metal vessel itself for its resale value.
The following morning, a young girl named Gerardina Amato discovered the scattered Hosts and immediately alerted the parish priest, Father Pasquale Allegro.
Sixty-three Hosts in all were recovered from where the thieves had left them, and rather than being consumed in the ordinary manner, they were set aside for observation.
A formal decree issued exactly a year later, on July 25, 1970, ordered that the recovered Hosts be kept under perpetual adoration in the church of San Mauro.
In 1994, the Hosts underwent formal scientific evaluation.

Under normal conditions, the unleavened wheat flour of a consecrated Host would be expected to deteriorate significantly within six months and largely disintegrate within a few years; these Hosts showed no such decay after twenty-five years.
Bishop Biagio D'Agostino of Vallo della Lucania, having reviewed the results, determined the preservation to be miraculous.

More than half a century after the theft, the Hosts remain incorrupt in the parish church of San Mauro Martire, described by local sources as the most recently recognized Eucharistic miracle in Italy at the time of its formal approval.
Like the Onil and Silla accounts from Spain in the same broad tradition, San Mauro La Bruca rests its case on sustained, later-tested physical preservation.
It does not rest on any single dramatic event: a theft meant to strip a church of value was undone by what the thieves chose to discard.
